enfranchisement

/en-FRAN-chyz-ment/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Enfranchisement means the granting of a formal right or privilege, especially the right to vote.

In 1920, the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment completed the enfranchisement of American women, millions of whom cast their first ballots that November.

Example

New Zealand made history in 1893 when its enfranchisement of women gave them the vote a full generation before most other nations followed.

The sentence shows enfranchisement as the formal granting of a right — here, a government officially extending the vote to a group that previously lacked it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

empowerment: Empowerment is the broad gaining of power, confidence, or standing, by any route — education, money, organizing. Enfranchisement is one precise legal event: the formal grant of a right, above all the vote. A community can feel empowered without winning any new right; enfranchisement puts the right on the books.

authorization: An authorization is official permission for one specific act — to access a file, to make one purchase — and it can expire or be revoked. Enfranchisement confers a lasting right that belongs to the citizen from then on. Authorization borrows power for a moment; enfranchisement grants it for good.

naturalization: Naturalization is the formal grant of citizenship itself to someone born elsewhere, an entire legal status with many rights bundled inside. Enfranchisement is narrower: the grant of one civic right, especially the vote. Naturalization usually brings enfranchisement with it, but a group can be enfranchised without any citizenship changing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

exclusion: Exclusion shuts a person out of participation — the condition enfranchisement is designed to end.

suppression: Suppression actively holds down a group's rights or voice rather than extending them.

Where it sits · how sweeping the granted liberty is

permission → enfranchisement → emancipation

permission vs. enfranchisement: Permission grants a small, revocable allowance for one activity, while enfranchisement confers a lasting formal right that belongs to the citizen.

emancipation vs. enfranchisement: Emancipation goes even further than enfranchisement, freeing a person from bondage or control entirely rather than granting one civic right.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — en-: to put into a state; to make

Root — -franchise-: free; freedom

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together: Put the pieces together and the word tells its own story: en- means to put someone into a state, the Old French root franc means 'free,' and -ment turns the action into a noun naming its result. Enfranchisement is literally 'the process of being made free' — and in modern English, that freedom is civic: being handed the formal rights of a full member of society, above all the right to vote.

Use the root in a new word: franchise: Reformers spent a decade campaigning to widen the franchise beyond property-owning men.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / historical-civic

Enfranchisement appears mostly in historical, legal, and political writing about voting rights and citizenship. Watch its near-twin disenfranchisement — the same word with dis- bolted on — which means the exact opposite: the stripping away of those rights.
